title: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
raw_sub: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs & Reparameterization Trick)
definition: A VAE (Kingma & Welling, 2013) is a directed probabilistic generative model that encodes input $\mathbf{x}$ into mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and variance $\log\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2$ parameters of a continuous Gaussian latent distribution, trained using the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) and Reparameterization Trick.
formula_explanation: The reparameterization trick moves the stochastic random sampling $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ outside the backpropagation graph, allowing deterministic gradients to flow back into encoder parameters $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$.
logic: The KL divergence regularizer forces the latent space to be dense, continuous, and centered at the unit Gaussian, allowing smooth interpolation between points to generate novel samples.
example: Latent face interpolation: moving smoothly along a vector between 'smiling face' and 'neutral face' in latent space generates natural gradual transitions.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
raw_sub: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs: Generator vs Discriminator)
definition: GANs (Goodfellow et al., 2014) frame generation as a two-player zero-sum minimax game between a Generator $G$ (which tries to produce realistic synthetic data from noise) and a Discriminator $D$ (which tries to distinguish real training samples from fake generated ones).
formula: $$\min_{G} \max_{D} V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{data}}[\log D(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log(1 - D(G(\mathbf{z})))]$$
formula_explanation: $D(\mathbf{x}) \in [0, 1]$ outputs probability that $\mathbf{x}$ is real. $G(\mathbf{z})$ maps Gaussian noise $\mathbf{z}$ to realistic synthetic data.
logic: At Nash equilibrium, the generator captures the true data distribution $p_g = p_{data}$, and the discriminator is unable to tell real from synthetic data ($D(\mathbf{x}) = 0.5$).
example: StyleGAN2 generating photorealistic 1024x1024 synthetic human faces that are indistinguishable from real photographs.

title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
raw_sub: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
definition: DDPM (Sohl-Dickstein 2015, Ho et al. 2020) generates high-fidelity data through a two-phase Markov process: a Forward Process that systematically destroys an image by adding Gaussian noise over $T$ steps, and a learned Reverse Process (a U-Net) that predicts and subtracts that noise step-by-step.
formula_explanation: $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ is the actual added Gaussian noise, and $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$ is the U-Net's estimate of the noise present at timestep $t$.
logic: Unlike GANs which suffer from mode collapse and training instability, diffusion models have stable convex-like regression objectives and cover the full multimodal distribution.
example: Starting with pure TV static white noise $\mathbf{x}_{1000}$, running 50 reverse denoising steps with a trained U-Net reconstructs a crystal-clear photorealistic landscape image.

title: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG)
raw_sub: Classifier-Free Guidance (Balancing prompt adherence vs diversity)
definition: Classifier-Free Guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2021) controls how strictly a generative diffusion model adheres to a text prompt versus sample diversity by interpolating between conditional noise predictions and unconditional (empty prompt) noise predictions.
formula_explanation: $c$ is the text prompt conditioning embedding, $\emptyset$ is the unconditional null token, and $s \ge 1.0$ is the guidance scale hyperparameter.
logic: Setting $s = 1.0$ yields standard conditioning. Raising $s$ to $7.0$ amplifies the direction where prompt features are strongest, dramatically boosting prompt faithfulness and image sharpness at the cost of diversity.
example: In Stable Diffusion or Midjourney: CFG scale $s = 7.5$ ensures an astronaut helmet prompt strictly renders a helmet instead of blending into general space backgrounds.

title: Latent Diffusion Models (LDM / Stable Diffusion)
raw_sub: Latent Diffusion Models (Running diffusion inside compressed latent space)
definition: Latent Diffusion Models (Rombach et al., 2022) train and execute the denoising diffusion process within a low-dimensional compressed latent space $\mathbf{z} = \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})$ learned by a pre-trained VAE, rather than directly on high-dimensional raw pixel space.
formula_explanation: For a $512 \times 512 \times 3$ image (786,432 numbers), compression factor $f=8$ yields a compact latent tensor of $64 \times 64 \times 4$ (16,384 numbers), an exact $48\times$ reduction in computational complexity.
logic: High-frequency imperceptible pixel noise is abstracted away by the VAE autoencoder, allowing the diffusion U-Net to concentrate its parameter capacity solely on semantic composition and geometry.
example: Stable Diffusion v1.5, SDXL, and Flux run diffusion on latents in seconds on consumer GPUs with 8GB VRAM, whereas pixel-space diffusion (Imagen) requires server clusters.

title: Subword Tokenization (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece)
raw_sub: Tokenizers (Byte-Pair Encoding BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece)
definition: Subword tokenization breaks arbitrary text into vocabulary chunks (subwords, characters, or byte sequences) balancing vocabulary size and sequence length, completely eliminating Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) tokens by merging frequent character pairs iteratively.
formula_explanation: BPE greedily merges the most frequent byte pair in each iteration until vocabulary size reaches target $V$ (e.g. 32k to 128k tokens).
logic: Character tokenization makes sequences too long for attention; whole-word tokenization causes vocabulary explosion and fails on novel words. Subword tokenization represents common words ('learning') as single tokens and rare words ('hyperparameter') as composite subwords ('hyper', 'parameter').
example: In GPT-4 (tiktoken `cl100k_base`): 'antigravity' is tokenized into two subwords: `['anti', 'gravity']`, preserving semantic morphology.

title: Dense Vector Embeddings & Semantic Geometry
raw_sub: Dense Vector Embeddings (Semantic clustering)
definition: Dense vector embeddings map discrete tokens, sentences, or documents into continuous real-valued geometric vector spaces $\mathbb{R}^d$ where cosine similarity captures deep semantic and functional relatedness.
formula_explanation: When vectors are L2-normalized ($\|\mathbf{u}\|_2 = 1$), cosine similarity simplifies directly to the inner dot product $\mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{v}$.
logic: Embeddings solve the curse of one-hot sparsity. In embedding space, vector arithmetic exhibits semantic linearity: $\mathbf{v}_{king} - \mathbf{v}_{man} + \mathbf{v}_{woman} \approx \mathbf{v}_{queen}$.
example: Text embeddings: 'cardiac arrest' and 'heart attack' share zero overlapping words, but their OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` vectors have cosine similarity $> 0.92$.

raw_subtopic: Context Window Scaling (YaRN, LongLoRA & StreamingLLM)
raw_sub: Context Window Scaling (YaRN, LongLoRA & StreamingLLM)
def: Architectures and mathematical interpolation strategies that extrapolate the effective context horizon of Transformer models beyond their initial pre-training window (e.g. 4k to 128k+) through RoPE frequency scaling, shifted sparse attention, and initial token attention sinks.
definition: Architectures and mathematical interpolation strategies that extrapolate the effective context horizon of Transformer models beyond their initial pre-training window (e.g. 4k to 128k+) through RoPE frequency scaling, shifted sparse attention, and initial token attention sinks.
logic: Direct positional extrapolation causes attention logits to explode because novel relative distances were never observed during training. YaRN interpolates high-frequency dimensions while extrapolating low frequencies to preserve local sharpness and global distance awareness.
core_logic: Direct positional extrapolation causes attention logits to explode because novel relative distances were never observed during training. YaRN interpolates high-frequency dimensions while extrapolating low frequencies to preserve local sharpness and global distance awareness.
example: Processing entire codebases: Extending a Llama-3 8B model's context from 8,192 tokens to 131,072 tokens to ingest complete git repositories and multi-file dependencies in a single inference call.
simple_summary: Transformers originally forget or break if you give them prompts longer than their training limit. Context scaling techniques gently stretch their position numbers so they can read entire books and giant codebases without retraining from scratch.

core_terms.what_is_it: Interpolation compresses position numbers into the known training range [0, L]; extrapolation assigns brand new unobserved numbers > L.

core_terms.what_is_it: A method that splits RoPE dimensions: high frequencies (local token grammar) stay untouched, while low frequencies (long-range topic order) are interpolated.
core_terms.analogy: Keeping the high-detail text on a road map crystal sharp, but zooming out the regional boundary scale.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Enables 128k context extension with only 400 steps of fine-tuning.

core_terms.what_is_it: The discovery that the first 4 tokens in any sequence absorb huge attention weight regardless of their semantics.
core_terms.analogy: A lightning rod on a roof that safely grounds excess electrical charge.

core_terms.what_is_it: Shifted short attention that divides long sequences into local groups and shifts them across half the heads to enable efficient fine-tuning.
core_terms.analogy: Relay race runners who only talk to their immediate handoff partners instead of yelling across the entire stadium.

title: Collaborative Filtering via Matrix Factorization Embeddings
raw_sub: Collaborative Filtering via Matrix Factorization Embeddings
definition: Matrix factorization decomposes a sparse user-item interaction matrix $\mathbf{R}$ into dense low-rank user embedding matrix $\mathbf{U}$ and item embedding matrix $\mathbf{V}$, capturing latent preferences and attributes for personalized recommendations.
formula_explanation: $r_{ui}$ is the observed rating/click, $\mathbf{u}_u \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is user $u$'s embedding, $\mathbf{v}_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is item $i$'s embedding, and $\lambda$ prevents overfitting.
logic: Users with similar viewing histories end up nearby in latent space. When user $A$ likes movies $X, Y$ and user $B$ likes $X, Y, Z$, user $A$'s dot product with movie $Z$ will be high, generating the recommendation.
example: Netflix / YouTube recommender systems: factorizing hundreds of millions of user watch records into 128-dimensional embedding vectors for instantaneous candidate retrieval.

title: Context Windows & Sequence Length Extrapolation
raw_sub: Context Windows & Sequence Length Extrapolation
definition: Context window defines the maximum sequence length an LLM can consume in a single forward pass. Extrapolation techniques (ALiBi, RoPE interpolation, LongLoRA) allow models pre-trained on short sequences to process 100k to 1M+ tokens without catastrophic perplexity explosion.
formula_explanation: ALiBi (Press et al., 2021) subtracts a linear penalty proportional to token distance $|i-j|$, with head-specific constant slope $m$.
logic: Standard self-attention memory scales quadratically $O(N^2)$ with token length $N$. RingAttention and Chunked FlashAttention distribute long context across GPU clusters to make 1-million-token prompts feasible.
example: Uploading a 500-page financial PDF into Gemini 1.5 Pro (2-million token context window) and asking targeted compliance questions across historical disclosures.

title: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) Projections
raw_sub: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) Vector Projections
definition: Self-attention transforms each input token embedding $\mathbf{x}$ into three distinct functional vector roles through learned linear projection weight matrices: Query $\mathbf{Q}$ (what I am looking for), Key $\mathbf{K}$ (what I contain), and Value $\mathbf{V}$ (the actual content payload).
formula_explanation: For input sequence $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_{model}}$, weight matrices $\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K, \mathbf{W}_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model} \times d_k}$ generate representations $\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_k}$.
logic: Decoupling Key and Value is the core innovation: the Key is optimized for indexing and matching against Queries, while the Value stores the raw semantic information transferred upon a match.
example: In a database search analogy: a search query string is $\mathbf{Q}$, column index titles are $\mathbf{K}$, and row table contents returned are $\mathbf{V}$.

title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
raw_sub: Scaled Dot-Product Attention & Temperature Scaling (√d_k)
definition: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) computes token relevance weights by taking dot products between queries and keys, dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ to prevent variance explosion, applying softmax, and computing a weighted sum of values.
formula_explanation: $d_k$ is the dimensionality of query/key vectors. If components have zero mean and unit variance, the dot product $\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}$ has variance $d_k$; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance.
logic: Without the scaling factor $\sqrt{d_k}$, large dimensions (e.g. $d_k = 128$) produce huge dot products, pushing Softmax into regions with near-zero gradients (vanishing gradient saturation).
example: With $d_k=64$, $\sqrt{d_k}=8$. If $\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k} = 32.0$, scaling rescales it to $4.0$, keeping Softmax gradients alive and informative.
raw_subtopic: Scaled Dot-Product Attention & Temperature Scaling (√d_k)

simple_summary: Scaled Dot-Product Attention is the engine of ChatGPT. It compares what a word is looking for (Query) with what other words offer (Key), scores how well they match, and gathers their information (Value).

numerical_example:
Suppose Key dimension d_k = 64, so √d_k = 8.
1. Raw dot product between word 'bank' and word 'river' = 32.0.
2. Divide by √d_k: 32.0 / 8 = 4.0.
3. Softmax turns 4.0 into a high attention probability (e.g. 0.85 or 85%).
4. 85% of 'river's Value vector is blended into 'bank', clarifying that 'bank' means a riverbank, not a money vault!

title: Multi-Head Attention (MHA)
raw_sub: Multi-Head Attention (MHA for diverse linguistic perspectives)
definition: Multi-Head Attention projects Queries, Keys, and Values into $h$ separate representation subspaces in parallel, allowing the model to attend simultaneously to information from different representation positions and semantic perspectives.
formula_explanation: $h$ is number of heads (typically 32 to 128), head dimension is $d_k = \frac{d_{model}}{h}$, and $\mathbf{W}_O \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{model} \times d_{model}}$ fuses head outputs.
logic: A single attention head can only focus on one type of relationship (e.g. grammatical subject). Multiple heads allow one head to track syntax, another to resolve pronoun coreference, and another to capture semantic tone.
example: In 'The dog didn't cross the street because *it* was too tired': Head 3 links 'it' to 'dog', while Head 7 links 'cross' to 'street'.

title: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
raw_sub: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA to compress KV-cache memory)
definition: Grouped-Query Attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) interpolates between Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA) by sharing single Key and Value heads across groups of Query heads, dramatically compressing KV-cache memory during autoregressive inference.
formula_explanation: $H_Q$ is query heads, $H_{KV}$ is key-value heads. Each group of $G$ query heads attends to the identical shared KV projection.
logic: During LLM generation, caching Keys and Values dominates GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM). GQA with $G=8$ reduces KV-cache memory bandwidth by $8\times$ with negligible quality loss.
example: LLaMA-3 70B and Mistral 7B utilize GQA with 8 KV heads: enables serving $8\times$ larger concurrent user batch sizes on a single GPU without running out of VRAM.

title: Causal Masking (Autoregressive Attention)
raw_sub: Causal Masking (Preventing future token visibility in autoregression)
definition: Causal masking enforces the arrow of time in decoder-only autoregressive LLMs by setting the upper triangular elements of the pre-softmax attention score matrix to $-\infty$, preventing token $t$ from looking ahead to tokens at $t+1, t+2, \dots$.
formula_explanation: Because $e^{-\infty} = 0$, applying Softmax assigns exactly 0% attention probability to all future token positions.
logic: Causal masking allows training on an entire prompt-and-response sequence of length $N$ in parallel during a single matrix multiplication pass, while strictly emulating step-by-step autoregressive generation.
example: When predicting word 4 in 'The cat sat on [?]', causal masking ensures the network only attends to tokens 1, 2, and 3, preventing data leakage.

title: Self-Supervised Pre-training (Causal LM)
raw_sub: Self-Supervised Pre-training (Next Token Prediction / Causal LM)
definition: Self-supervised pre-training trains a massive base neural network on trillions of tokens of raw internet text using Next-Token Prediction (Causal Language Modeling), forcing the model to absorb world knowledge, logic, and grammar without human labels.
formula_explanation: $x_t$ is the target token at position $t$ from the vocabulary, and $P_\theta$ is the predicted probability assigned to that token given preceding context.
logic: Language is a compression of human intelligence. In order to accurately predict the next word across millions of science textbooks, code repositories, and philosophical treatises, the model must build internal world simulators.
example: Pre-training LLaMA-3: consuming 15 trillion tokens across 16,384 H100 GPUs over several months, resulting in an encyclopedic foundation model.

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT / Instruction Tuning)
raw_sub: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT on question-answer instructions)
definition: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) transforms a raw autocomplete base model into an interactive conversational assistant by training on curated high-quality pairs of user prompts (instructions) and target assistant responses.
formula_explanation: Loss is computed strictly on response tokens ($t > L_{prompt}$); prompt tokens are masked out so the model is only penalized for response quality.
logic: The 'Superficial Alignment Hypothesis' (LIMA paper): almost all knowledge is learned during pre-training; SFT merely teaches the model the formatting style and conversational tone to surface that knowledge.
example: Prompt: 'Write a Python script to scrape an RSS feed.' Target response: 'Here is how you can use feedparser...'. Loss guides weights to produce helpful assistant behavior.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
raw_sub: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
definition: PEFT freezes the overwhelming majority (99%+) of pre-trained LLM weights and only trains a tiny set of auxiliary parameters (e.g. adapter layers, prompt tuning tokens, or low-rank matrices), reducing memory requirements by orders of magnitude.
formula_explanation: Gradients and optimizer states (which take $12-16$ bytes per parameter in Adam) are only stored for $\boldsymbol{\phi}$.
logic: Full fine-tuning of a 70B model requires ~1,100 GB of VRAM across multiple 80GB GPUs. PEFT allows fine-tuning that same 70B model on a single 48GB GPU by updating only 50M parameters.
example: Prefix Tuning, Adapters, and LoRA: training domain-specific adaptations for medical radiology reports without altering the base model.

title: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
raw_sub: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation with rank r decomposition)
definition: LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) freezes pre-trained weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ and parameterizes its weight update delta $\Delta \mathbf{W}$ as the product of two low-rank matrices $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$, where rank $r \ll \min(d, k)$.
formula_explanation: $r$ is low rank (e.g. 8 or 16). $\mathbf{B}$ initialized to 0 ensures $\Delta \mathbf{W} = 0$ at step 0. $\alpha$ is a constant scaling hyperparameter.
logic: The intrinsic rank of weight deltas during downstream fine-tuning is extremely small. Factorizing into rank 16 matrices reduces trainable parameters by $10,000\times$. At inference, $\Delta \mathbf{W}$ can be permanently folded back into $\mathbf{W}_0$ with zero added latency.
example: Fine-tuning a $4096 \times 4096$ projection ($16.7$M parameters): rank $r=8$ decomposition requires only $(4096 \times 8) + (8 \times 4096) = 65,536$ parameters ($0.39\%$ of original).

title: QLoRA (Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation)
raw_sub: QLoRA (4-bit NormalFloat quantization + Paged Optimizers)
definition: QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), backpropagates gradients through the 4-bit weights into 16-bit LoRA adapters, and uses Paged Optimizers to manage memory spikes.
formula_explanation: NF4 is an information-theoretically optimal quantile quantization for normally distributed neural network weights.
logic: Base model weights are held in 4-bit memory (compressing a 65B model from 130GB down to under 35GB), and only unquantized high-precision LoRA adapters are updated.
example: Fine-tuning a 65-billion parameter model on a single consumer NVIDIA RTX 3090/4090 GPU (24GB VRAM) over a weekend.

title: Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
raw_sub: Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
definition: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when fine-tuning an LLM on a narrow new domain (e.g. legal text) causes it to abruptly lose pre-trained general reasoning, coding, or mathematical competencies learned during pre-training.
formula_explanation: Mitigated using Experience Replay (mixing 5-10% general pre-training data into fine-tuning) or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) penalizing changes to critical parameters weighted by Fisher Information $F_i$.
logic: Fine-tuning updates weights along the gradient of the new task without constraint, inadvertently destroying delicate high-dimensional manifolds representing general reasoning.
example: Fine-tuning a coding model on Python: without mixing in math and conversational replay data, its ability to solve GSM8K math reasoning drops by 40%.

title: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)
raw_sub: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback via PPO)
definition: RLHF aligns language model outputs with human intent (Helpful, Honest, Harmless) by training a Reward Model $r_\psi(x, y)$ on human preference comparisons, then optimizing the LLM policy $\pi_\theta$ via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).
formula_explanation: $r_\psi(x, y)$ is the scalar reward score, and the KL divergence penalty $\beta D_{KL}$ prevents the model policy $\pi_\theta$ from straying too far from original base policy $\pi_{ref}$ (reward hacking).
logic: Human evaluation of quality is easy to judge comparatively ($y_1 > y_2$) but hard to write an explicit calculus loss function for. RLHF bridges human intuitive preference into gradient optimization.
example: Turning InstructGPT and ChatGPT from toxic or rambly text completers into polite, well-structured, safe conversational assistants.

raw_sub: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization on paired responses)
definition: DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) mathematically proves that the constrained RLHF objective can be solved exactly via an implicit reward function, eliminating the need to train a separate reward model or run unstable PPO reinforcement learning loops.
formula_explanation: $y_w$ is the human-preferred 'winning' answer, $y_l$ is the 'losing' rejected answer, and $\beta$ controls KL regularization strength.
logic: DPO reduces alignment to a simple binary cross-entropy classification loss directly over pairs of responses, providing immense mathematical stability and reducing GPU compute requirements by 3-5x compared to PPO.
example: Used to align modern open models like Zephyr-7B, Starling-LM, and LLaMA-3 Instruct directly on paired preference datasets.

title: Constitutional AI & RLAIF
raw_sub: Constitutional AI & Automated Self-Correction
definition: Constitutional AI (Anthropic, Bai et al., 2022) replaces expensive human feedback with Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF), using a written set of natural-language principles ('a constitution') to have the model critique and revise its own responses.
formula: $$\text{Step 1: Critique: } c \sim \text{LLM}(x, y, \text{Principle}) \quad \to \quad \text{Step 2: Revision: } y^* \sim \text{LLM}(x, y, c)$$
formula_explanation: Principles enforce rules like 'Choose the response that is less harmful and avoids assisting dangerous activities.'
logic: Human annotators are slow, expensive, and introduce personal biases. Constitutional AI allows alignment to scale transparently, with explicit public governance rules governing behavior.
example: Powering Claude 3: constitutional principles instruct the model to politely decline producing malware while remaining maximally helpful for cybersecurity defense analysis.

title: Knowledge Distillation (Teacher-Student)
raw_sub: Knowledge Distillation (Teacher model soft labels train student)
definition: Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) transfers the reasoning capacity of a massive teacher model (e.g. 405B) into a compact, lightweight student model (e.g. 8B) by training the student to match the teacher's softened output probability distribution.
formula_explanation: $\mathbf{z}_t$ and $\mathbf{z}_s$ are teacher and student logits, $T$ is softmax temperature smoothing probabilities, and $\alpha$ balances ground truth vs teacher alignment.
logic: The teacher's 'dark knowledge' (secondary probabilities over incorrect tokens, e.g. knowing a cat is closer to a tiger than a car) provides immensely richer learning signals than hard 0/1 labels.
example: DistilBERT (60% size of BERT, retains 97% performance) and LLaMA-3.1 8B fine-tuned using synthetic outputs generated by LLaMA-3.1 405B.

title: Model Quantization (AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF)
raw_sub: Model Quantization (FP16 -> INT8 / INT4 via AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF)
definition: Quantization compresses model parameter weights from 16-bit floating point (FP16/BF16) down to 8-bit or 4-bit integers (INT8/INT4), slashing GPU memory footprint by $4\times$ and accelerating memory-bound autoregressive decoding throughput.
formula_explanation: $S$ is the FP16 scale factor and $Z$ is zero-point integer offset. AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) protects the 1% most salient weight channels based on activation magnitudes.
logic: Autoregressive generation is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Fetching 4-bit weights from VRAM to compute cores takes $25\%$ of the time compared to 16-bit weights.
example: Running LLaMA-3 8B: in FP16 it requires 16GB VRAM; quantized via GGUF (Q4_K_M) it requires only 4.8GB RAM, running comfortably on a MacBook or iPhone.

title: Document Parsing & Chunking Strategies
raw_sub: Document Parsing & Chunking (Fixed-size, Recursive, Semantic)
definition: Chunking breaks large documents into optimal discrete segments for vector retrieval. Strategies include Fixed-Size Chunking (character count with overlap), Recursive Character Splitting (respecting paragraphs and code fences), and Semantic Chunking (splitting when semantic embedding similarity shifts).
formula_explanation: Sliding window overlap ensures sentences cut in half at chunk boundaries retain full semantic context in at least one chunk.
logic: If chunks are too small (e.g. 50 tokens), they lack sufficient surrounding context. If chunks are too large (e.g. 4000 tokens), specific factual details are diluted across general narrative in embedding space.
example:
In LangChain / LlamaIndex: `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200, separators=['

', '
', ' ', ''])` keeps headers and paragraphs intact.

title: Vector Databases & Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)
raw_sub: Vector Databases (Chroma, Pinecone, Milvus, Qdrant, FAISS)
definition: Vector databases store, index, and query multi-dimensional dense embeddings at scale using Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search algorithms like HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) and Inverted File Index (IVF).
formula: $$\text{HNSW Complexity: } O(\log N) \quad \text{vs Flat Exact Search: } O(N \cdot d)$$
formula_explanation: $N$ is total vectors stored and $d$ is embedding dimension. Multi-layer proximity skip-graphs enable searching 100M vectors in under 5 milliseconds.
logic: Exact brute-force cosine distance search requires computing dot products against every document in the database, which becomes impossible at enterprise scale.
example: Using Pinecone, Qdrant, or Chroma to store 2 million enterprise HR policies and querying the top 5 most relevant snippets in 12ms.

title: Hybrid Search (Dense + Sparse BM25 Fusion)
raw_sub: Hybrid Search (Dense Vector Cosine + Sparse BM25 Keyword Search)
definition: Hybrid search combines the semantic conceptual understanding of dense vector embeddings with the exact keyword matching precision of sparse lexical search (BM25 / SPLADE), fused using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
formula_explanation: $\text{rank}_m(d)$ is the 1-based rank position of document $d$ in system $m$, and $k$ is a smoothing constant.
logic: Dense embeddings often fail on exact alphanumeric identifiers (part numbers, serial codes, drug names 'XYZ-9021'). BM25 nails exact strings, while dense vectors nail conceptual synonyms ('head pain' $\to$ 'migraine').
example: Searching medical records for patient 'ID-99412 allergy penicillin': BM25 guarantees finding the exact ID, while dense search surfaces relevant clinical allergy documentation.

title: Cross-Encoder Re-ranking
raw_sub: Cross-Encoder Re-ranking (Rescoring candidate chunks)
definition: Re-ranking uses a two-stage retrieval pipeline: a fast bi-encoder (vector DB) retrieves top $K=50$ candidates, which are then passed through an intensive cross-encoder model (e.g. Cohere Rerank, BGE-Reranker) that performs joint full self-attention across prompt and passage pairs.
formula_explanation: Cross-encoders evaluate all pairwise token interactions between query and candidate document simultaneously, yielding dramatically higher semantic accuracy.
logic: Bi-encoders compress an entire 500-word document into a single fixed vector, inherently losing fine nuance. Cross-encoders examine every word of query against every word of chunk.
example: In an enterprise RAG pipeline: vector search fetches 40 candidates; Cross-Encoder rescores and filters down to the top 3 truly authoritative passages, boosting factual accuracy by 25%.

title: Hallucination Mitigation & Source Grounding
raw_sub: Hallucination Mitigation & Source Grounding
definition: Techniques to ensure an LLM generates answers strictly grounded in retrieved evidence rather than fabricating plausible-sounding falsehoods from parametric memory. Includes citation linking, chain-of-verification, and RAG triad evaluation (Context Relevance, Groundedness, Answer Relevance).
formula: $$\text{Faithfulness Score} = \frac{|\text{Claims in Answer supported by Context}|}{|\text{Total Claims in Answer}|} \in [0, 1]$$

title: Zero-shot & Few-shot In-Context Learning
raw_sub: Zero-shot & Few-shot In-Context Learning
definition: In-Context Learning (Brown et al., 2020) allows pre-trained LLMs to execute new tasks without parameter weight updates simply by conditioning on task instructions (Zero-shot) or a few input-output demonstration pairs (Few-shot) inside the prompt.
formula_explanation: $k$ is the number of exemplars (shots). In-context attention mechanisms infer latent task functions directly on the forward pass activations.
logic: Few-shot examples steer model activations into the desired output distribution and format (e.g. valid JSON) without triggering catastrophic forgetting or fine-tuning infrastructure costs.
example: Prompting: 'Translate English to SQL. Input: show active users -> Output: SELECT * FROM users WHERE active=1; Input: count orders -> Output: [Model completes correctly]'.

title: Chain of Thought (CoT Reasoning)
raw_sub: Chain of Thought (CoT - 'Let's think step by step')
definition: Chain of Thought (Wei et al., 2022) prompts language models to decompose complex multi-step reasoning problems into intermediate natural language deduction steps before arriving at a final answer (e.g. 'Let's think step by step').
formula_explanation: Allocates intermediate test-time compute tokens, expanding the working computational budget of the transformer forward passes.
logic: Transformers perform a fixed amount of computation per output token. Asking for an instant answer forces a 1-step guess. Generating intermediate thought tokens allows the model to store partial state and work through algorithmic logic.
example: Math word problem: 'A store has 15 apples. It sells 6, buys 10, then drops 2. How many are left?' CoT writes out $15-6=9 \to 9+10=19 \to 19-2=17$, avoiding careless arithmetic errors.

title: ReAct Framework (Reasoning + Acting)
raw_sub: ReAct Framework (Reasoning + Acting in iterative loops)
definition: The ReAct framework (Yao et al., 2022) combines reasoning traces and task-specific external tool actions in an interleaved loop: Thought (verbal reason about situation) $\to$ Action (call tool) $\to$ Observation (receive tool output) $\to$ Repeat until goal is achieved.
formula_explanation: $\tau_t$ is the historical context trace, augmented with each new observation to ground subsequent reasoning steps.
logic: Pure reasoning models suffer from hallucination and lack current environment information. Pure action models lack strategic long-term planning. ReAct combines dynamic thought planning with environmental feedback.
example: Agent looking up weather: Thought: 'I need current temperature in Tokyo.' Action: `weather_api('Tokyo')`. Observation: `'22°C, Rain'`. Thought: 'Now I should advise an umbrella.' Final Response: 'It is 22°C and rainy in Tokyo, bring an umbrella!'

title: Function Calling & Tool Use
raw_sub: Function Calling & Tool Use (APIs, Code Interpreters, SQL)
definition: Function calling equips LLMs with JSON schemas defining available software tools (APIs, databases, bash shells, calculators). The model generates structured machine-readable JSON function calls instead of text, which an executor environment runs and returns results for.
formula_explanation: Fine-tuned models strictly conform to JSON Schema specifications, enabling reliable deterministic software integration.
logic: Allows models to break out of the static knowledge frozen at training time, performing real-world actions like running unit tests, sending emails, or querying live SQL databases.
example: User asks: 'Calculate $893 \times 4291$'. Instead of guessing, the LLM emits a function call `python_interpreter(expr='893 * 4291')`, receiving exact answer `3831863`.

title: Agent Memory Architectures
raw_sub: Agent Memory (Short-term working context + Long-term vector memory)
definition: Agent memory architectures divide state storage into Short-term Memory (the active conversational context window and scratchpad) and Long-term Memory (an external vector database storing episodic past experiences and semantic user profiles retrieved via similarity).
formula_explanation: Past experiences are retrieved using a scoring function combining Recency, Importance, and Semantic Relevance (Park et al., 2023).
logic: Context windows are limited and transient. Long-term memory allows autonomous agents to remember user preferences across sessions, learn from past trial-and-error mistakes, and maintain coherent persona.
example: Personal coding assistant recalling: 'User prefers type annotations and pytest syntax' from a conversation held three weeks prior.

title: High-Throughput Serving & PagedAttention (vLLM)
raw_sub: High-Throughput Serving (vLLM PagedAttention, TensorRT-LLM, ONNX)
definition: Production inference optimization technologies that maximize GPU hardware utilization. PagedAttention (vLLM - Kwon et al., 2023) manages LLM Key-Value cache memory like virtual memory pages in operating systems, eliminating internal and external fragmentation.
formula_explanation: Continuous iteration-level batching dynamically injects new requests as soon as finished requests complete, without waiting for batch completion.
logic: Standard LLM serving pre-allocates contiguous memory for maximum possible sequence lengths (e.g. 4096 tokens), leaving huge empty memory gaps. PagedAttention allocates blocks dynamically on demand.
example: vLLM serves 20-30x more tokens per second per GPU compared to standard Hugging Face Transformers, enabling economical production scale.

title: Data Drift vs Concept Drift Monitoring
raw_sub: Data Drift vs Concept Drift Monitoring (PSI, KS-Test)
definition: Data Drift refers to shifts in the input feature distribution $P(X)$ over time while relationship $P(Y|X)$ remains constant. Concept Drift occurs when the true statistical relationship between inputs and targets $P(Y|X)$ changes due to macroeconomic or real-world shifts.
formula_explanation: Population Stability Index (PSI): $\text{PSI} < 0.1$ indicates stability, $> 0.25$ indicates significant drift requiring model retraining. KS is Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
logic: Models trained on static historical data inevitably decay in accuracy as consumer habits, inflation, or seasons change. Automated drift alarms trigger automated retraining pipelines.
example: E-commerce spending during COVID-19 lockdown: purchase behavior shifted overnight. Concept drift rendered previous fraud detection models inaccurate until retrained.

definition: A feature store (e.g. Feast, Hopsworks) provides a unified data platform with a dual interface: low-latency key-value storage (Redis) for real-time online inference, and distributed storage (Snowflake/BigQuery) with point-in-time time-travel joins for offline training.

formula: $$\text{Demographic Parity: } P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=0) = P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=1)$$ $$\text{Equalized Odds: } P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=0, Y=y) = P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid A=1, Y=y)$$
formula_explanation: $A \in \{0, 1\}$ is a protected demographic attribute (gender, ethnicity, age) and $Y$ is the ground truth outcome.
logic: Models trained on historical data frequently reproduce historical socio-economic inequities. Formal auditing ensures algorithmic fairness before models are approved for lending, hiring, or healthcare.
example: Using Fairlearn or AIF360 to audit loan approval algorithms, ensuring qualified applicants receive equal acceptance rates regardless of gender.

title: Human & Cognitive Biases (Reporting, Historical, Automation & Confirmation Bias)
simple_summary: Machine learning models do not invent bias out of thin air; they inherit, codify, and magnify human cognitive blind spots, real-world historical prejudices, and the tendency for humans to over-trust automated outputs.
core_logic: When training an AI model, data is a historical record of human actions and language. If historical data contains discrimination, reporting omissions, or evaluator biases, a neural network optimizes to reproduce those exact biases with high mathematical confidence.
definition_bullets: Historical Bias: Occurs when existing cultural prejudices, socio-economic inequalities, or outdated practices in the real world are accurately captured in data, causing models to replicate and perpetuate past injustices.

Reporting Bias: Arises when the frequency of events, outcomes, or words in data does not reflect their true real-world frequency, because people predominantly write about unusual or noteworthy occurrences while omitting mundane facts.

Automation Bias: The psychological tendency for human operators and evaluators to favor suggestions made by automated AI decision systems over human judgment, even when the automated system is demonstrably incorrect.

Confirmation Bias: The tendency for model developers and evaluators to search for, interpret, and favor data and test slices that confirm their preexisting hypotheses while dismissing evidence of model failure.
Implicit Bias: Unconscious associations, stereotypes, and automatic assumptions held by annotators and engineers that subtly shape dataset labeling guidelines and feature selection.
Experimenter's Bias: Occurs when a model evaluator or researcher continues testing and tuning until a desired benchmark result is produced, effectively cherry-picking positive metrics.

core_terms.what_is_it: Bias embedded in the real-world conditions from which data is gathered, even if the data sampling itself is mathematically perfect.
core_terms.analogy: If historical job data reflects that 95% of Fortune 500 CEOs were men, an AI resume screener will learn to penalize female resumes even if gender was never explicitly intended as a factor.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Shows why accurate historical data does not equal fair or ethical AI predictions.

core_terms.what_is_it: A distortion where people capture and write about rare or extreme events far more often than common, baseline events.
core_terms.analogy: People post online when their flight is delayed or their restaurant meal is awful, but rarely post when a flight arrives exactly on time. A model trained on tweets would conclude all airplanes are perpetually delayed.
core_terms.why_it_matters: NLP models trained on web text develop skewed beliefs about real-world probability distributions.

core_terms.what_is_it: Humans blindly trusting computer algorithm outputs over their own expert judgment or common sense.
core_terms.analogy: A driver blindly following a GPS system onto a closed bridge or into a lake, ignoring giant physical road closure warning signs.
core_terms.why_it_matters: In medical and legal AI, doctors or judges may rubber-stamp flawed model recommendations without scrutiny.

core_terms.what_is_it: Cherry-picking test data or prompts that confirm the developer's belief that their model is working properly.
core_terms.analogy: A student who only takes practice quiz questions they know they can answer, falsely concluding they are prepared for the final exam.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Causes unsafe models to pass internal reviews and reach production before their critical flaws are uncovered.

symbol_guide.meaning: True ground-truth outcome in the real world
symbol_guide.plain_english: The actual capability or qualification of an applicant

symbol_guide.meaning: Model prediction for a protected demographic cohort
symbol_guide.plain_english: The automated score assigned by the algorithm to a specific group
The mean predicted probability across all cohort members

numerical_example:
Consider a hiring tool evaluating 100 male and 100 female applicants of identical qualifications.
1. Due to Historical Bias in training text, male keywords ('varsity', 'captain') score higher than neutral keywords.
2. Model approves 82 out of 100 male applicants (82%).
3. Model approves only 44 out of 100 female applicants (44%).
4. Disparity Ratio: 44% / 82% = 0.536 (violates the standard 80% four-fifths fairness rule).
Conclusion: The model codified past hiring disparities into an automated barrier.
architectural_logic: Deep neural networks are universal function approximators that minimize loss by seizing on any correlating feature. When protected attributes correlate with historical labels, the network learns non-zero weights or embedding directions that encode social bias.
example: Amazon's automated resume screening tool: Trained on 10 years of historical tech applicant resumes, the system learned to penalize resumes containing the word 'women's' (e.g. 'women's chess club captain') because historical hires had been predominantly male.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Removing protected labels (like gender or race) does NOT remove bias! Deep networks easily reconstruct protected attributes from proxy features such as zip codes, schools attended, or linguistic word choice.
key_takeaways: Data is a mirror of historical human behavior, capturing past prejudices.
Reporting bias causes rare events to be overrepresented in web-scale text datasets.
Automation bias leads human evaluators to over-rely on flawed algorithmic suggestions.
Fairness requires active metric tracking, not passive feature exclusion.

title: Selection Bias (Coverage, Non-Response & Sampling Bias)
simple_summary: Selection bias occurs when the sample population gathered for training does not accurately represent the real-world population the model will serve in production.
core_logic: If certain user groups are systematically excluded from data collection, or if people who respond to surveys differ fundamentally from those who do not, the resulting model performs brilliantly on the sampled subset while failing silently on excluded demographics.
definition_bullets: Selection Bias: Systematic error introduced when the sample population chosen for dataset training does not accurately represent the target population intended for production deployment.

Coverage Bias: Occurs when certain subgroups of the population are systematically excluded or omitted from the data collection frame (e.g. training a smartphone health app exclusively on users with high-end flagship phones).
Non-Response Bias: Arises when individuals who choose not to participate in surveys or feedback forms have fundamentally different characteristics and satisfaction levels than those who do respond.
Sampling Bias: Occurs when data collection methods inadvertently over-sample specific convenient demographics (convenience sampling) while under-sampling rare or harder-to-reach cohorts.

core_terms.what_is_it: When the collection mechanism physically cannot reach certain subsets of the population.
core_terms.analogy: Conducting a public opinion poll exclusively by calling landline telephone numbers; young adults who only own mobile phones have 0% chance of being covered.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Creates blind spots where models have zero training signals for entire user groups.

core_terms.what_is_it: When respondents differ systematically from non-respondents.
core_terms.analogy: Only extremely angry or extremely thrilled customers leave online restaurant reviews. Moderate, satisfied customers rarely leave reviews, skewing the sentiment dataset into bipolar extremes.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Distorts real-world feature distributions and labels.

core_terms.what_is_it: Over-representing convenient groups during dataset creation.
core_terms.analogy: Training a self-driving car vision model using dashcam video recorded exclusively in sunny California, leaving the model unprepared for snow or night driving.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Causes models to fail critically when exposed to unrepresented environmental conditions.

symbol_guide.plain_english: Whether an instance was included in the training dataset

symbol_guide.meaning: Probability distribution of sampled training data
symbol_guide.plain_english: What the AI sees during training
What exists in the actual real-world population

numerical_example:
A survey of 1,000 hospital patients has a 20% response rate.
1. Out of 200 respondents, 180 (90%) report high satisfaction.
2. Investigation of the 800 non-respondents reveals 600 did not respond because their health worsened.
3. True satisfaction across all 1,000 patients: (180 + 200) / 1,000 = 38%.
Conclusion: Relying only on respondents yielded a 90% satisfaction claim when the true reality was 38%!
architectural_logic: Supervised loss functions compute expected loss over the empirical training distribution P_emp(X, Y). If sampling probabilities deviate from true population rates, gradient descent minimizes loss for the oversampled majority at the expense of under-represented minorities.
example: Medical diagnostic imaging: Computer vision models for melanoma detection trained predominantly on light-skinned patient photos exhibit significantly lower diagnostic accuracy when tested on darker skin tones due to coverage bias in academic dermatology datasets.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Assuming more data solves sampling bias! If you collect 10 million more data points using the same biased collection pipeline, you only become 10 million times more confident in an inaccurate representation.
key_takeaways: Selection bias means training samples diverge from the true production population.
Coverage bias creates blind spots by excluding subgroups from data collection.
Non-response bias skews datasets toward vocal or extreme participants.
More data does not fix sampling bias; demographic stratified sampling does.

title: Fairness Metrics (Demographic Parity, Equality of Opportunity & Counterfactual Fairness)
simple_summary: Fairness cannot be defined in a single universal equation. Different mathematical metrics define fairness differently: equal positive outcomes (Demographic Parity), equal accuracy on qualified individuals (Equality of Opportunity), or invariant predictions under hypothetical attribute changes (Counterfactual Fairness).
core_logic: Depending on legal, ethical, and clinical requirements, different fairness metrics are mathematically incompatible. Choosing the right fairness definition requires understanding the tradeoffs between outcome parity and predictive accuracy.
definition_bullets: Demographic Parity (Statistical Parity): Requires that the probability of receiving a favorable outcome (Ŷ = 1) is identical across all protected demographic groups, regardless of true label distributions: P(Ŷ=1 | A=0) = P(Ŷ=1 | A=1).
Equality of Opportunity: Focuses on qualified individuals, requiring that the True Positive Rate (Recall) is identical across groups: P(Ŷ=1 | Y=1, A=0) = P(Ŷ=1 | Y=1, A=1).

Counterfactual Fairness: Requires that a model's prediction for an individual would remain exactly the same if their protected demographic attribute (e.g., race, gender) were hypothetically changed, holding non-protected causal factors constant.

Fairness Impossibility Theorem: Proves mathematically that Demographic Parity, Equality of Opportunity, and Predictive Parity cannot be simultaneously satisfied whenever base true disease/risk rates differ across demographic groups.

core_terms.what_is_it: Equal acceptance rates across all demographic groups regardless of qualification base rates.
core_terms.analogy: Admitting exactly 50% men and 50% women to a coding bootcamp, regardless of the applicant pool demographics.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Enforces systemic equality of outcomes to remedy historical exclusion.

core_terms.what_is_it: Equal true positive rates: anyone qualified has an equal chance of being selected, regardless of group.
core_terms.analogy: If two students both know the subject matter equally well (Y=1), both have an identical 90% probability of passing the automated exam.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Standard metric in credit scoring and job recruiting under anti-discrimination laws.

core_terms.what_is_it: Causal invariance: flipping a demographic bit in the causal graph produces zero change in output.
core_terms.analogy: Reviewing an identical resume where only the name at the top is changed from 'James' to 'Jamal', verifying the model generates the identical ranking score.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Prevents causal discrimination by testing hypothetical parallel universes.

formula: P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=1, A=0) = P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid Y=1, A=1)

symbol_guide.plain_english: e.g. Loan approved or candidate hired
e.g. The candidate actually repaid the loan or succeeded at the job
e.g. Cohort A vs Cohort B

numerical_example:
Consider 100 qualified candidates in Group 0 and 100 qualified candidates in Group 1.
1. In Group 0, model approves 80 qualified candidates (TPR = 80 / 100 = 0.80).
2. In Group 1, model approves 60 qualified candidates (TPR = 60 / 100 = 0.60).
3. Equality of Opportunity Discrepancy: |0.80 - 0.60| = 0.20.
4. To satisfy Equality of Opportunity, the decision threshold for Group 1 must be adjusted until its TPR reaches 0.80.
architectural_logic: In constrained optimization, fairness metrics are added to the loss function as Lagrangian multipliers or penalties, forcing backpropagation to trade small amounts of raw training accuracy for equalized true positive rates across groups.
example: FICO credit scoring: Regulators evaluate whether automated credit scoring models maintain equal True Positive Rates across demographic cohorts under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Thinking you can achieve ALL fairness metrics at once! Kleinberg's theorem proves you mathematically cannot satisfy Demographic Parity, Equal TPR, and Equal Calibration simultaneously if base rates differ.
key_takeaways: Demographic parity demands equal positive prediction rates across groups.
Equality of opportunity demands equal true positive rates for qualified candidates.
Counterfactual fairness requires predictions to remain unchanged if protected attributes were flipped.
Fairness metrics often conflict; engineering teams must choose criteria based on domain ethics.

title: Algorithmic Bias Mitigation (MinDiff & Counterfactual Logit Pairing)
simple_summary: Algorithmic bias mitigation refers to explicit mathematical techniques added during data preprocessing, loss computation, or post-inference thresholding to eradicate unfair disparities.
core_logic: Standard gradient descent only cares about minimizing overall training loss, which allows the model to exploit easy stereotyping shortcuts. By adding regularization penalties like MinDiff or Counterfactual Logit Pairing, we force the network to learn invariant representations.
definition_bullets: MinDiff Optimization: A training-time regularization technique that penalizes the difference in prediction score distributions between a privileged group and an unprivileged group on non-targeted examples, pushing distributions into alignment.

Counterfactual Logit Pairing (CLP): An adversarial training technique that feeds two counterfactual examples (e.g., 'He is an engineer' vs 'She is an engineer') through the network and penalizes any divergence between their raw output logits.
Pre-processing Mitigation: Debiasing raw data through re-weighting, targeted oversampling of underrepresented cohorts, or synthetic augmentation before training begins.
Post-processing Threshold Tuning: Setting group-specific decision thresholds on classification probability curves to equalize True Positive Rates or False Positive Rates without retraining the model.

core_terms.what_is_it: A loss penalty minimizing divergence between score distributions across groups.
core_terms.analogy: Aligning two test grade curves so that equally qualified groups produce matching probability distributions.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Enables models to reduce disparate impact without sacrificing core predictive task performance.

core_terms.what_is_it: Penalizing differences between raw logits of twin examples differing only by a sensitive attribute.
core_terms.analogy: Testing twin essays where only pronouns are swapped; if the model gives different grades, the grading engine is penalized until both match.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Directly enforces counterfactual fairness inside neural network representations.

core_terms.what_is_it: Adjusting decision thresholds (e.g. 0.45 for Group A, 0.55 for Group B) to ensure equalized True Positive Rates.
core_terms.analogy: Calibrating two different thermometers so both read exactly 100°C at boiling water.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Fast post-processing fix when retraining large foundation models is too expensive.

symbol_guide.plain_english: How well the model performs its main task
The distance between two probability distributions
Controls how heavily the model prioritizes fairness vs accuracy

numerical_example:
1. Standard Cross-Entropy Loss: L_task = 0.32.
2. Disparity between privileged and unprivileged score distributions: MMD = 0.18.
3. Fairness regularizer weight: λ = 0.5.
4. Total Loss: L_total = 0.32 + (0.5 × 0.18) = 0.32 + 0.09 = 0.41.
5. Backpropagation computes gradients to decrease both prediction error and distribution disparity.
architectural_logic: CLP attaches an auxiliary loss head during the forward pass: L_CLP = ||logit(x) - logit(x')||_2. Gradients force the intermediate hidden layers to purge sensitive demographic signals from their internal embedding manifolds.
example: Toxicity classification in online comments: Google Perspective API used Counterfactual Logit Pairing to ensure identity terms (e.g. 'I am a gay man') produced the exact same non-toxic score as 'I am a straight man'.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Setting the fairness regularizer λ too high! An excessively high λ forces the model to ignore all useful features, flattening predictions into a useless uniform distribution.
key_takeaways: MinDiff penalizes distribution differences between privileged and unprivileged groups.
Counterfactual Logit Pairing forces identical logits when only protected terms are swapped.
Preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing offer three distinct intervention layers.
Threshold tuning allows post-processing fairness adjustments without retraining.

title: Training-Serving Skew & Label Leakage
simple_summary: Training-serving skew occurs when offline training conditions differ from live production reality. Label leakage is the catastrophic mistake of including information in training features that will not exist at the exact moment of live inference.
core_logic: A model evaluated in a notebook has access to clean historical databases. In production, features must be served in milliseconds over network calls. When feature engineering pipelines differ between training and serving, or when future outcome data leaks into features, models achieve 99% training accuracy and immediately crash in production.
definition_bullets: Training-Serving Skew: A dangerous divergence in performance where a model achieves outstanding accuracy during offline training but degrades catastrophically in production due to differences in data pipelines, feature transformations, or timing.

Label Leakage (Target Leakage): Occurs when features available during training contain direct clues or causal consequences of the target label that will never be available at the exact instant of live inference.

Feature Drift & Schema Inconsistencies: When production feature values shift over time (e.g., inflation changes monetary scales) or upstream API schemas change without alerting the ML serving pipeline.
Feedback Loops: When a model's own production decisions alter future incoming training data (e.g. YouTube recommendation algorithm training on clicks from its own past recommendations).

core_terms.what_is_it: Performance difference caused by discrepancies in data handling between training time and serving time.
core_terms.analogy: Studying for a medical exam with open-book notes, but being forced to take the actual licensing exam in a closed-book locked room.
core_terms.why_it_matters: The #1 cause of machine learning projects failing after production deployment.

core_terms.what_is_it: Accidentally including features that were recorded after or caused by the target outcome.
core_terms.analogy: Predicting whether a hospital patient has pneumonia using a feature called 'Pneumonia Antibiotic Prescribed'. The model gets 100% accuracy, but is completely useless for early diagnosis.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Creates deceptively perfect validation metrics that collapse in live deployment.

core_terms.what_is_it: Ensuring every training row only uses feature values that existed at or before that exact event timestamp.
core_terms.analogy: Rewinding a security camera to 2:00 PM and only using clues visible at 2:00 PM to guess who will enter at 2:05 PM.
core_terms.why_it_matters: The core architectural principle behind modern Feature Stores like Feast and Tecton.

symbol_guide.meaning: Probability distribution of features during training
symbol_guide.plain_english: What your training batch looks like

symbol_guide.meaning: Probability distribution of features during live serving
symbol_guide.plain_english: What live user requests look like
Measures how much the serving distribution has drifted from training

numerical_example:
1. Training Accuracy in Jupyter Notebook: 99.4% (using feature 'transaction_refund_status').
2. In live production, refund status is only populated 3 days AFTER a fraudulent purchase occurs.
3. Live production accuracy drops to 52.1% (random guessing).
Conclusion: The feature leaked the target label, creating an artificial 99% metric offline.
architectural_logic: Production ML systems enforce a single shared transformation pipeline (e.g. tf.transform or Feast Feature Store) compiled into a C++ or Rust binary, ensuring training and online serving execute identical code on raw features.
example: E-commerce fraud prevention: Training on database tables that include account closure timestamps that occurred after the fraud event, leading the model to rely on features that don't exist during live checkout.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Calculating feature scaling (like StandardScaler mean and std) on the combined dataset before splitting train and test! Always fit scalers ONLY on training data to prevent data leakage.
key_takeaways: Training-serving skew causes models with high training metrics to fail in production.
Label leakage happens when training features contain clues from the future.
Use a shared Feature Store to guarantee identical feature logic between training and serving.
Always enforce strict point-in-time timestamp joins when building training sets.

title: Data Slices, Sliced Metrics & The Unicorn Model Antipattern
simple_summary: Evaluating an AI model only on aggregate top-line accuracy is dangerous because a 95% overall score can easily hide a 0% failure rate on critical demographic cohorts or high-risk edge cases. The 'Unicorn Model' is the mythical antipattern of expecting one global model to solve all problems universally.
core_logic: Aggregate metrics (like global AUC or mean accuracy) are dominated by common, frequent data points. Sliced evaluation breaks down performance across distinct subsets to verify reliability where failure is expensive.
definition_bullets: Data Slices: Subsets of a dataset partitioned by specific categorical features, demographic cohorts, geographical locations, or temporal windows (e.g., users in rural regions with low-bandwidth connections).

Sliced Evaluation: The mandatory practice of evaluating model accuracy, loss, and latency separately across each data slice, preventing aggregate top-line metrics from masking catastrophic failure on critical cohorts.

The Unicorn Model Antipattern: The misguided assumption that a single, monolithic 'unicorn' model can optimally handle wildly disparate tasks, countries, languages, or modalities simultaneously without localized tuning or modular decomposition.
Disaggregated Metrics: Reporting metrics (AUC, F1, Latency) across high-risk slices (e.g. night-time driving in autonomous vehicles) to enforce hard reliability bounds before production deployment.

core_terms.what_is_it: Specific subsets of data grouped by meaningful dimensions (e.g. device type, region, time of day).
core_terms.analogy: Evaluating crash safety not just on an 'average adult dummy', but separately on child car seats, elderly passengers, and pregnant drivers.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Identifies localized weaknesses that global averages completely conceal.

core_terms.what_is_it: The antipattern of building one massive model to handle everything instead of specialized modular systems.
core_terms.analogy: Trying to build a single vehicle that is simultaneously a Formula 1 racecar, a submarine, and a cargo freight truck.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Modular architectures (or Mixture of Experts) consistently outperform over-stretched single models in production.

core_terms.what_is_it: Publishing model cards with performance broken down across all audited user cohorts.
core_terms.analogy: A nutrition label listing vitamins, fats, and sugars separately rather than just printing a single 'healthiness score'.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Required by ethical AI guidelines and enterprise auditing standards.

symbol_guide.plain_english: e.g. Users browsing on Android in India

symbol_guide.meaning: Count of examples in slice k
symbol_guide.plain_english: Total samples belonging to this subgroup
Loss on example i

numerical_example:
1. Overall dataset: 10,000 users. Overall Accuracy: 96.0% (9,600 / 10,000).
2. Slice A (Desktop Users, 9,000 samples): Accuracy = 99.0% (8,910 correct).
3. Slice B (Mobile Users with low bandwidth, 1,000 samples): Accuracy = 69.0% (690 correct).
Conclusion: The high desktop accuracy disguised that the mobile experience is broken (31% failure rate)!
architectural_logic: Production evaluation frameworks (such as TensorFlow Model Analysis - TFMA) automatically compute metrics across combinations of feature slices using Apache Beam, blocking automated CI/CD deployments if any single slice drops below threshold.
example: Autonomous vehicle perception: A pedestrian detector achieving 98% overall accuracy fails completely on the slice 'Pedestrians wearing dark clothing at night in rain', demonstrating why sliced validation is life-critical.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Only checking overall F1 score or accuracy. Always inspect slices for under-represented demographics, low-end device types, and seasonal extremes.
key_takeaways: Overall accuracy can hide 0% performance on critical minority slices.
Sliced evaluation tests model reliability on granular sub-cohorts.
The Unicorn Model antipattern attempts to force one model to solve mismatched tasks.
Production pipelines must enforce minimum metric thresholds across all slices.

title: Static vs Dynamic Training & Static vs Dynamic Inference
simple_summary: Machine learning systems must choose between static (offline, precomputed, stable) and dynamic (online, real-time, responsive) paradigms for both model training and live prediction inference.
core_logic: Training can be static (trained once on historical data) or dynamic (continuously updated with streaming events). Inference can be static (precomputed batch predictions stored in cache) or dynamic (computed on-demand per HTTP request). Selecting the wrong combination wastes cloud compute or serves stale predictions.
definition_bullets: Static Training (Offline Training): The model is trained once on historical batch data and deployed as an immutable artifact. Easy to verify and monitor, but becomes stale as real-world distributions drift.

Dynamic Training (Online Continuous Training): The model continuously updates its weights in real time or hourly batches as new streaming data arrives, preventing obsolescence but requiring automated safeguards against rogue updates.

Static Inference (Batch Offline Prediction): Predictions are computed in advance for all users (e.g. overnight batch recommendation table) and written to a fast cache (Redis). Ultra-low latency and cheap, but cannot react to immediate real-time user context.

Dynamic Inference (Online Real-Time Serving): Predictions are generated on-demand as incoming HTTP requests arrive. Incorporates immediate real-time features, but requires low-latency serving infrastructure and GPU auto-scaling.

core_terms.what_is_it: Training a model once in a batch job and deploying the fixed weights.
core_terms.analogy: Printing an encyclopedia book; the facts are thoroughly verified before printing, but it cannot include events that happened yesterday.
core_terms.why_it_matters: High stability, predictable costs, and simple governance.

core_terms.what_is_it: Continuously adapting model weights on streaming data.
core_terms.analogy: A financial trader adjusting stock bets minute-by-minute as market news flashes across the terminal.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Essential for high-velocity domains like ad-click prediction and viral content feeds.

core_terms.what_is_it: Precomputing predictions in batch and storing them in a key-value database.
core_terms.analogy: A restaurant chef preparing 100 sandwiches before the lunch rush; serving takes 2 seconds, but you can't customize toppings.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Achieves sub-5ms latency and eliminates GPU scaling costs during peak traffic.

core_terms.what_is_it: Running the neural network forward pass in real-time for each incoming request.
core_terms.analogy: A custom chef making an omelet to order after asking exactly what ingredients you want right now.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Required when inputs are novel user prompts, images, or real-time location data.

symbol_guide.plain_english: Fetching a precomputed prediction from Redis cache in 2 milliseconds
Total mathematical operations required to run the neural network forward pass
How many tokens or inferences the GPU can process per second

numerical_example:
1. Netflix recommendation system with 200 million users.
2. Static Inference: Run batch pipeline overnight across 200M users. Store top 50 movie IDs in Redis. At login, fetching recommendations takes 3ms.
3. Dynamic Inference: If Netflix computed deep transformer passes on-demand at every user login, it would require 50,000 GPUs running concurrently.
Conclusion: Hybrid architecture precomputes candidate pools statically, then re-ranks the top 100 dynamically.
architectural_logic: Production systems often adopt a two-stage hybrid: an offline batch process generates candidate IDs (Static Inference), followed by a lightweight online model that re-scores candidates with the user's latest session clicks (Dynamic Inference).
example: Spam filtering: Static training runs weekly on verified spam archives. Dynamic inference classifies incoming emails on the fly within 50 milliseconds using live header features.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Defaulting to dynamic real-time inference when static precomputed inference is 100x cheaper and 10x faster for finite user bases with predictable catalog items.
key_takeaways: Static training is offline, stable, and verified; dynamic training updates continuously.
Static inference precomputes outputs for fast caching; dynamic inference computes on demand.
Use static inference when input spaces are finite and low latency is critical.
Production recommendation systems often combine static candidate retrieval with dynamic re-ranking.

title: Text Preprocessing, Lemmatization, Stopwords & Linguistic Normalization
raw_subtopic: Text Preprocessing, Lemmatization, Stopwords & Linguistic Normalization
raw_sub: Text Preprocessing, Lemmatization, Stopwords & Linguistic Normalization
def: The foundational pipeline of transforming raw unstructured text strings into standardized linguistic units through case folding, Unicode normalization (NFC/NFKD), regex cleaning, morphological lemmatization, and selective stopword removal.
definition: The foundational pipeline of transforming raw unstructured text strings into standardized linguistic units through case folding, Unicode normalization (NFC/NFKD), regex cleaning, morphological lemmatization, and selective stopword removal.
logic: Raw text contains noise, dialectal variants, and inflectional inflections ('running', 'runs', 'ran'). Normalization collapses inflectional redundancy to a canonical vocabulary base.
core_logic: Raw text contains noise, dialectal variants, and inflectional inflections ('running', 'runs', 'ran'). Normalization collapses inflectional redundancy to a canonical vocabulary base.
example: Legal discovery search: Mapping 'contractual obligations', 'contracted', and 'contracting' to the common lemma 'contract' so semantic search surfaces all relevant clauses regardless of grammatical tense.
simple_summary: Before feeding human writing into NLP models, text preprocessing strips out weird formatting, turns words into their dictionary root forms (like turning 'mice' into 'mouse'), and cleans away filler words.

core_terms.what_is_it: Using linguistic vocabulary and morphological analysis to return words to their canonical dictionary lemma (e.g. 'better' -> 'good', 'was' -> 'be').
core_terms.analogy: Tracing branches of a family tree back to the common grandparent root.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Unlike crude suffix-chopping stemming (which turns 'universe' into 'univers'), lemmatization always produces real, valid root words.

core_terms.what_is_it: Rule-based heuristic chopping of word endings (Porter/Snowball stemmers) to approximate root form.
core_terms.analogy: Using hedge clippers to cut the ends off hedges without checking the botany.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Extremely fast, but produces non-words like 'organ' from 'organization' and 'organism'.

core_terms.what_is_it: High-frequency syntactic glue words ('the', 'is', 'at', 'which') that carry little topical information in classic search.
core_terms.analogy: The filler words ('um', 'uh', 'like') in everyday spoken conversation.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Removing them reduces index size by 30-40% in BM25/TF-IDF (though modern LLMs keep them for full syntax).

core_terms.what_is_it: Decomposing ligature glyphs, accents, and special symbols into standard compatible ASCII/Unicode code points.
core_terms.analogy: Converting fancy calligraphy curly letters into plain typewriter alphabet.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Prevents 'café' (composed) and 'cafe\u0301' (decomposed) from being treated as two totally different words.

symbol_guide.meaning: Set of stopword tokens to exclude
symbol_guide.plain_english: e.g. {'the', 'a', 'in', 'on'}
Standardizes accented characters and symbols

numerical_example: Raw: 'The CEO's 3 cafes were thriving!'. Unicode/Regex: 'the ceos 3 cafes were thriving'. Stopwords removed: 'ceos 3 cafes thriving'. Lemmatized: 'ceo 3 cafe thrive'. Vocabulary size for this phrase drops from 7 tokens to 4 canonical root concepts.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Blindly removing stopwords when training sentiment analysis models or modern LLMs. The word 'not' is on standard stopword lists, but removing it flips 'not good' into 'good', completely reversing the sentiment!
definition_bullets: Lemmatization: Using linguistic vocabulary to return words to their canonical dictionary lemma.
Stemming: Rule-based heuristic chopping of word endings to approximate root form.
Stopwords: High-frequency syntactic glue words that carry little topical information in search.
Unicode Normalization: Decomposing ligature glyphs and accents into standard compatible code points.

title: N-Grams, Bigrams & Statistical Language Modeling
simple_summary: Before deep learning, language was modeled statistically using N-grams: counting how often sequences of N consecutive words appear together to calculate the probability of the next word.
core_logic: An N-gram model estimates the probability of word w_t given the preceding N-1 words. By applying the Markov assumption, long historical dependencies are truncated to local windows, allowing fast probability lookups using frequency counts.
definition_bullets: N-Gram: A contiguous sequence of N items (words or characters) extracted from a text corpus. N=1 is a Unigram, N=2 is a Bigram, N=3 is a Trigram.

Statistical Language Model: A probability distribution over sequences of words, calculating the probability of a sentence P(w_1, ..., w_T) or predicting the next token P(w_t | w_{t-1}, ..., w_{t-N+1}).
Markov Assumption: The simplifying assumption that the probability of the next word depends only on the preceding N-1 words, rather than the entire historical context of the text.
Smoothing & Zero-Frequency Problem: Techniques like Laplace or Kneser-Ney smoothing that allocate small probability mass to unseen word combinations to prevent multiplication by zero.

core_terms.what_is_it: A two-word sequence (N=2) predicting the next word based exclusively on the single preceding word.
core_terms.analogy: After hearing 'ice', predicting 'cream' with 90% probability and 'fire' with 0.1% probability.
core_terms.why_it_matters: The simplest statistical language model.

core_terms.what_is_it: Assuming only the last N-1 words matter for predicting the next word.
core_terms.analogy: Driving looking only 10 feet ahead through the windshield, ignoring the map of the route behind you.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Makes language computation tractable, but prevents understanding long-term narrative context.

core_terms.what_is_it: The standard metric measuring how surprised a language model is by real text.
core_terms.analogy: A multiple-choice quiz where the model is confused between 10 equally likely choices (Perplexity = 10). Lower is better.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Evaluates language models across both N-gram and modern LLM paradigms.

symbol_guide.meaning: How many times the pair appeared together
symbol_guide.plain_english: e.g. Count('san', 'francisco')

symbol_guide.meaning: How many times the first word appeared alone
symbol_guide.plain_english: e.g. Count('san')
Probability of 'francisco' given 'san'

numerical_example:
In a corpus of text:
1. 'artificial intelligence' appears 400 times.
2. 'artificial' appears 500 times total.
3. Probability P('intelligence' | 'artificial') = 400 / 500 = 0.80 (80%).
4. 'artificial flowers' appears 50 times. P('flowers' | 'artificial') = 50 / 500 = 0.10 (10%).
Conclusion: Given 'artificial', the model predicts 'intelligence' as 8x more likely than 'flowers'.
architectural_logic: N-gram models store transition tables in hash maps. As N increases (e.g. 5-grams), the state space grows exponentially (V^N), causing severe sparsity where 99% of valid phrases have zero counts, motivating neural language models.
example: Smartphone keyboard autocomplete: Mobile keyboards use lightweight cached N-gram models to suggest the next 3 words in real time with zero latency and low battery drain.
pitfalls: Common Pitfall: Forgetting smoothing! If a test sentence contains a single 2-word phrase that never appeared in training, the unsmoothed bigram probability evaluates to 0.0, zeroing out the probability of the entire sentence.
key_takeaways: N-grams predict the next word using frequency counts of preceding words.
Bigrams look back 1 word; Trigrams look back 2 words.
The Markov assumption limits memory to a short local context window.
Perplexity measures how uncertain the model is when predicting words (lower is better).

title: Sparse vs Dense Representations & Word2Vec (Skip-Gram & CBOW)
simple_summary: Sparse vectors (one-hot) treat words as isolated, orthogonal IDs with zero semantic relation. Word2Vec solved this by learning dense continuous vectors where words with similar meanings cluster together in geometric space.
core_logic: Based on the distributional hypothesis ('a word is characterized by the company it keeps'), Word2Vec trains a shallow 2-layer neural network on text corpora to predict context words from center words (Skip-Gram) or center words from context (CBOW). In doing so, the hidden layer weights become rich semantic embeddings.
definition_bullets: Sparse Representations (One-Hot & Bag-of-Words): High-dimensional vectors (size = vocabulary size V, e.g. 50,000) containing almost all zeros with a single 1. Orthogonal by definition, meaning 'dog' and 'puppy' have zero mathematical similarity.
Dense Word Embeddings: Low-dimensional continuous vectors (e.g. 300 to 1,536 dimensions) where every value is non-zero, capturing latent semantic meaning and conceptual proximity.
